definition: Of machine prose: fluent, confident and wrong; possessing the rhythm of sense without the substance.
etymology: A blend of faux (French, ‘false’) and fluent (Latin fluere, ‘to flow’). The seam falls on the shared glide — say it aloud and the false part has slipped past before you can object, which is rather the point.
in_use: The report was flawlessly fauxluent — beautifully paragraphed nonsense.
the_case: Every name we have for the false fact points at the citation and never at the prose around it — the cadence that carried a nothing across your desk without a wobble. Fauxluent points there instead, and because it is an adjective you can apply it before you have checked: a flag rather than a verdict. Behind it is the bargain the machine has broken. Fluency used to be evidence because it was expensive, earned by years of thinking about the thing; it is free now, and free things stop being evidence.
seo_title: fauxluent — when AI writing reads perfectly and is wrong
seo_description: The summary moved; the case was cited by name and year; there was no case. Fauxluent names prose with the rhythm of sense and none of the substance.
